paper_information.title: Diseases of Lentil
paper_information.journal_or_source: Handbook of Vegetable and Herb Diseases, Handbook of Plant Disease Management, Springer Nature Switzerland AG
paper_information.abstract_summary: This chapter discusses several economically important lentil diseases with special reference to their distribution and impact, biology and epidemiology, and integrated disease management approaches, covering fungal, bacterial, viral, and nematode diseases.
paper_information.research_objective: Provide comprehensive knowledge on lentil diseases, their geographical occurrence, disease pathology, and explore management strategies to mitigate yield and quality losses.
important_findings: Fungal diseases like Fusarium wilt, Stemphylium blight, and Ascochyta blight are major biotic constraints causing heavy yield losses globally.
Various other fungal, bacterial, viral, and nematode diseases threaten lentil production under varying climatic conditions.
Integrated disease management utilizing cultural, biological, chemical, and genetic resistance approaches is essential for sustainable lentil production.

diseases.causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. lentis Shlecht. emend. Snyder and Hansen f. sp. lentis Vasud. and Srini

general: Patches of wilted plants appear in the field at seedling and adult stages
Wilting of leaves resembling water deficiency
Stunting and shrinking of plants
Curling of leaves from lower parts moving progressively up the stem
early_symptoms: Sudden drooping and drying of plants resulting in seedling death
advanced_symptoms: Dark brown discoloration in the xylem tissue of roots and stems visible upon vertical splitting
visual_field_symptoms: Patches of wilted plants in the field

field_identification: Patches of wilted plants
Dark brown discoloration of root and stem xylem tissue when split vertically
diagnostic_methods: Screening tests under field trials, greenhouses, and laboratory settings

causes_and_risk_factors: Warm soil temperatures and dry soil conditions
Synergistic interaction with plant-pathogenic nematodes like Ditylenchus spp., Meloidogyne spp., and Pratylenchus spp.

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: Dry soil conditions, sandy loam soil compared to clay soil, soil pH up to 7.5

disease_development_and_spread: Fungal spores germinate and elongate towards host roots in response to plant signals
Penetration via natural openings or wounds, invading root cortex, epidermis, and reaching xylem vessels
Vertical growth, multiplication, and colonization in xylem until plant wilting
Transmission through plant debris, soil contamination, and seeds
severity_and_yield_loss: May cause 5-10% yield loss, but complete crop failure can occur under favorable conditions
Yield loss ranging from 9.6% to 100% and wilt incidence ranging from 20% to 46.67%

cultural_management: Ensuring use of clean and disease-free seeds
Planting seeds at proper depth around 10-12 cm
Deep plowing and removal of infected crop residues
Chemical amendments involving manganese and zinc
Selecting early maturing cultivars or adjusting planting time
biological_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma harzianum @ 6 g/kg seed

Use of antagonists like Pseudomonas fluorescens, Trichoderma viride, Bacillus velezensis, Streptomyces, Glomus coronatum, Gliocladium, Piriformospora indica, Sebacina vermafera, and Penicillium chrysogenum
Plant extracts of Azadirachta indica, Justicia adhatoda, Ficus religiosa, Carica papaya, Ricinus communis, Ficus benghalensis, Psidium guajava, and Tamarindus indica at concentrations above 15%

prevention: Use of clean and disease-free seeds

diseases.causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea Pers. ex Fr. and Botrytis fabae Sardiña

general: Dark green spots on lower foliage turning into pale tan-colored spots
Infected leaves and flowers deteriorate into rotting masses
Pods become seedless or deformed with undersized seeds
Lesions on stems are light brown or blanched, covered with gray mold, and rot at the crown
advanced_symptoms: Whole plant eventually becomes infected and dried out
visual_field_symptoms: Scattered pattern of dead plants in the field that rapidly spreads
Fuzzy spore masses and black sclerotia on infected stems

field_identification: Gray mold growth on stems, flowers, and pods
Scattered pattern of dead plants

favorable_conditions.rainfall: >20 mm for susceptible varieties, >40 mm for moderately susceptible varieties

disease_development_and_spread: Infection starts on flowers and pods
Conidia serve as sources of secondary infection dispersed through air
Survival through mycelium, sclerotia, and chlamydospores, as well as infected seeds
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield reduction from 30% to complete failure
Yield losses of more than 50% reported in Australia

cultural_management: Rotating fungicides with different modes of action
biological_management: Application of biocontrol agents such as Pseudomonas fluorescens, Pantoea agglomerans, Penicillium griseofulvum, Penicillium aurantiogriseum, Trichoderma hamatum, and Trichoderma harzianum

chemical_management.timing: mid-flower in early-seeded cultivars or early flower in late-seeded cultivars
chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: provided comparable efficacy to multiple applications

integrated_management: Combining foliar fungicides, seed treatments, resistant cultivars, physical treatments, and cultural methods

warnings_and_limitations: Fungicide resistance development in Botrytis cinerea poses a significant threat

general: Initial symptoms appear on upper canopy
Minute gray or light brown lesions on leaflets with pinhead-like appearance
Lesions undergo irregular enlargement and rapidly spread
Infected tissue appears light cream-colored with angular pattern
Infected stems dry up, exhibiting inverted J-shaped appearance and turning ashy white
advanced_symptoms: Significant defoliation leaving only terminal leaflets
Flower abortion and reduced seed germination rates
visual_field_symptoms: Completely blighted field appearance within 7-10 days
Field can appear as if burnt by fire

field_identification: Minute gray or light brown pinhead lesions on leaflets spreading rapidly
Inverted J-shaped ashy white stems

favorable_conditions.temperature: average mean temperature of 18 ± 2 °C (daytime above 22 °C, night around 8 °C)
other_conditions: Cloudy and foggy days (30-50 days per year)

disease_development_and_spread: Infection occurs primarily during reproductive stages
Airborne conidia act as secondary source of inoculum
Conidia germinate within 6 hours under moisture, entering via stomata or epidermal penetration
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses of up to 62% in Bangladesh, exceeding 90% in Bihar, India
Complete crop failure under highly favorable conditions

cultural_management: Delaying sowing or early sowing on November 1
biological_management: Application of botanicals derived from Acoros calamus and Zanthoxylum armatum
Use of Trichoderma viride and Trichoderma harzianum

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: effective disease control and increased lentil yield
effective disease control and increased lentil yield

diseases.causal_agent: Ascochyta lentis Bond. and Vassil, Teleomorph: Didymella lentis, syn. Ascochyta fabae f.sp. lentis Gossen, Sheard, Beauchamp & Morrall

general: Light gray spot-like lesions becoming tan-colored with dark brown margins
Tiny dark fruiting bodies (pycnidia) develop in lesion centers
advanced_symptoms: Stem girdling causing breakage and death of plant tissue above
Wilting and browning of stem tips
Flower and pod abortion, shriveled and discolored seeds

field_identification: Tan-colored lesions with dark brown margins and speckling pycnidia
Stem breakage from girdling lesions
diagnostic_methods: Molecular genetic marker technology (RAPDs, AFLPs, ISSRs, RFLPs, SSRs, SNPs)

causes_and_risk_factors: Infected seeds and leftover plant debris

favorable_conditions.rainfall: high levels of rainfall, wet winter conditions

disease_development_and_spread: Transmission through infected seeds or leftover plant debris
Airborne spores and rain-splash dispersal up to 15 cm
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses up to 40%, potentially exceeding 70% with severe seed staining and mold

cultural_management: Early seeding to avoid damp weather during harvest
biological_management: Use of biocontrol agents like Trichoderma harzianum, Beauveria bassiana, Metarhizium anisopliae, Lecanicillium lecanii, and Pseudomonas fluorescens (UmComb)

chemical_management.application_method: seed treatment followed by foliar sprays
chemical_management.timing: at the time of disease appearance
chemical_management.number_of_applications: 3 sprays of Bavistin (2 g/l) at 10-day intervals

integrated_management: Pre-soaking seeds in water at 20 °C for 6 hours followed by hot water immersion (53 °C for 15 min), seed treatment with Bavistin + Thiram, and foliar sprays

warnings_and_limitations: Effectiveness of resistance genes from ILL5588 has been lost, and isolates capable of overcoming key resistance genes have been identified

general: Seedlings exhibit high susceptibility and succumb rapidly
Mature plants gradually girdled by lesions leading to death
Dark-brown lesions on stem at or just beneath soil level
Lower leaves show dull or yellowish appearance followed by progressive wilting
advanced_symptoms: Abundant white fluffy mycelium on infected tissues and soil
Round sclerotia, size of black mustard seed, turning black after maturity
visual_field_symptoms: Disease symptoms seen in patches, but entire field affected in severe cases

field_identification: White fluffy mycelium and mustard-seed-like sclerotia on roots and soil
Collar rot and seedling collapse in patches

disease_development_and_spread: Survival as mycelium in infected tissues and plant debris or sclerotia in soil
Sclerotial germination via hyphal or eruptive germination
Dissemination via contaminated soil and tools, infested seedlings, water, wind, and seeds
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield loss ranges from 1% to 60% in fields

cultural_management: Adding organic amendments (cow dung, poultry refuse, oil cakes)
biological_management: Seed treatment with Trichoderma harzianum and Pseudomonas fluorescens

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: reduced foot and root rot incidence and higher yields

integrated_management: Combining organic amendments, oil cakes, biological control agents, and fungicide drenching

farmer_action_points: Treat seeds with Trichoderma harzianum and Pseudomonas fluorescens

general: Yellowish white pycnidia and aecial cups on lower surface of leaflets
Brown uredial pustules on both upper and lower surfaces of leaflets
Pustules oval to circular, up to 1 mm in diameter, coalescing
Dark brown to black elongated telia on branches and stems
advanced_symptoms: Premature shedding of leaves followed by premature drying of entire plant
No seed development or only small, shriveled seeds formed
visual_field_symptoms: Brown to blackish patches of the disease in the field

field_identification: Yellowish aecial cups and brown uredial pustules on leaves
Dark brown to black telia on stems

causes_and_risk_factors: Contaminated lentil seeds and infected plant debris
disease_development_and_spread: Automacrocyclic fungus completing entire life cycle on a single host
Teliospores and telia act as primary source of infection
Aeciospores play a crucial role in pathogen spread during growing season
Urediniospores cause long-distance dispersal and epidemics
severity_and_yield_loss: Yield losses ranging from 60% to 69%, up to 100% in countries like Ethiopia, Morocco, Chile, Ecuador, Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan

biological_management: Combination of fungicides with Trichoderma harzianum and Pseudomonas fluorescence
Inoculation with Rhizobium strains (LR-35-01, LRB-1, and LRB-2)

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: reducing rust severity and pod damage, improving yield
comparable efficacy to chemical fungicides in reducing rust severity

farmer_action_points: Use foliar fungicides like triazoles or mancozeb

diseases.causal_agent: Colletotrichum lentis (Damm) (syn C. truncatum (Schwein.)) Andrus and W.D

general: Small yellow spots on leaves progressing to greenish water-soaked lesions on lower leaves
Lesions turn tan-colored with varying oval shapes and sizes
Small, sunken, golden-brown stem lesions with black margins that expand and may encircle the stem
advanced_symptoms: Extensive stem girdling resulting in premature defoliation, disruption of water and nutrient uptake, wilting, and plant death
Acervuli form giving rise to abundant conidia and black microsclerotia causing marked blackening of old tissues
visual_field_symptoms: Large areas with brown and dying plants within the field

field_identification: Sunken golden-brown stem lesions with black margins
Blackened old tissues due to microsclerotia

disease_development_and_spread: Infection from spores present on debris or soil
Spreads upwards through rain splash
Microsclerotia act as resting stage surviving up to 5 years or more in soil
severity_and_yield_loss: Substantial yield losses of up to 60-70%

cultural_management: Crop rotation and tillage to break down infected stubble and microsclerotia
3-year field break from lentils by cultivating non-host crops like cereals and oil seeds
Planting new lentil crops at considerable distance from previous fields
Eliminating volunteer lentils and wild vetch
Soaking infested seeds in hot water at 52 °C for 30 min
biological_management: Trichoderma harzianum and Pseudomonas fluorescens used as seed treatments

chemical_management.timing: before flowering (10-12 node stage); repeat at 5-day intervals if conducive conditions persist

farmer_action_points: Frequent field scouting from seedling stage onwards
Apply foliar fungicides before fungus attacks stems

diseases.causal_agent: Erysiphe pisi DC., Erysiphe polygoni DC., Leveillula taurica (Lév.) Arnaud (also Erysiphe trifolii)

general: Tiny spots with fine powdery, white growth containing conidia and mycelium on upper surface of mature leaves
Extensive mycelial growth and conidial production covering leaves, stems, and pods
advanced_symptoms: Leaflets dry up, curl, and are shed prematurely, leaving only terminal leaves
Infected seeds remain small and shriveled
visual_field_symptoms: White powdery mass of spores easily rubbed off leaf surface

field_identification: White powdery fungal growth on leaves, stems, and pods

causes_and_risk_factors: Infected debris, leguminous weeds, or volunteer plants
disease_development_and_spread: Spread via anamorph spores
Survival on infected debris, weeds, or volunteer plants
severity_and_yield_loss: Significant yield loss from early infections

cultural_management: Employing overhead irrigation to wash fungus from leaves

chemical_management.active_ingredient_or_product: tridemorph, aqueous sulfur, karathane (dinocap), calixin, sulfex (ferrous bisulfide)
chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: effective in controlling and reducing powdery mildew growth

warnings_and_limitations: Can cause uneven crop maturation and harvesting difficulties as desiccants cannot penetrate dense fungal layer

diseases.causal_agent: Fusarium solani, Sclerotium rolfsii, Rhizoctonia solani, Rhizoctonia bataticola (Dry Root Rot), Pythium aphanidermatum, Pythium ultimum, Aphanomyces euteiches

general: Failure of seedlings to emerge
Light brown to red water-soaked roots and stems
Stunted plant growth
Rotting taproots with few lateral roots and absence of secondary roots
advanced_symptoms: Affected plants droop, become stunted, and eventually dry up and die
visual_field_symptoms: Appears in localized patches linked to flooding or prolonged waterlogging

field_identification: Localized patches of wilted/dying seedlings
Water-soaked roots and rotting taproots in waterlogged areas

causes_and_risk_factors: Soil-borne pathogen persistence in soil and debris

favorable_conditions.temperature: warm to hot, wet climates (Fusarium solani); warm, humid climates (S. rolfsii, Pythium); cool, wet climates (Rhizoctonia solani, Aphanomyces euteiches)
favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: well-drained sandy soils reduce disease incidence

disease_development_and_spread: Survival in soil, plant debris, and seeds as dormant mycelia, sclerotia, or spores
Root exudates from germinating seedlings stimulate dormant fungi
severity_and_yield_loss: Significant yield losses in susceptible varieties

chemical_management.result_reported_in_paper: proven effective for seed treatment, leading to disease reduction and increased seed yield
effective in controlling foot and root rot incidence

general: Brown circular lesion on leaves which may become dry and torn in the middle resembling 'shot holes'
visual_field_symptoms: Brown, circular and translucent foliar lesions

field_identification: Brown circular leaf lesions with shot-hole appearance

causes_and_risk_factors: Survival in seed or crop debris of host plants
disease_development_and_spread: Seed-borne or crop debris survival
severity_and_yield_loss: Reported as minor disease with 5% incidence in commercial fields in South Dakota

diseases.causal_agent: Meloidogyne incognita, Meloidogyne javanica, Meloidogyne artiella

general: Characteristic swellings known as galls on roots making roots appear knotted or distorted
advanced_symptoms: Wilting, stunting, necrosis of leaf edges, and chlorosis during moisture stress

field_identification: Root galls/knots distinguishable from Rhizobium nodules
differential_diagnosis: Nematode-induced galls become part of central root tissue, whereas Rhizobium nodules attach to the side of root hairs and detach easily

causes_and_risk_factors: J2 stage nematodes entering growing roots
disease_development_and_spread: J2 nematodes enter growing roots and branches, causing hyperplasia, hypertrophy, and giant cell formation
severity_and_yield_loss: Pulse crop yield losses estimated up to 20-35%; combination with wilt fungal disease drastically lowers production

cultural_management: Soil amendments (neem cake, mahua cake, groundnut cake, sunflower cake)
biological_management: Rhizobium sp. in conjunction with cow dung and eggshell powder
integrated_management: Combining oil cake (such as Mahua cake) with bioagents or lower dosage of nematicide

farmer_action_points: Apply organic soil amendments like neem cake or mahua cake
warnings_and_limitations: No cultivars of lentil resistant to root-knot nematodes are available in Europe

diseases.causal_agent: Pratylenchus lentis n. sp., Pratylenchus neglectus, Pratylenchus thornei, Pratylenchus hamatus

general: Small, dark-brown to black lesions along roots
Impeded root development and nutrient uptake
advanced_symptoms: Nutrient deficiency symptoms, chlorosis of leaves, and wilting during moisture stress
visual_field_symptoms: Dark-brown to black root lesions and reduced plant vigor

field_identification: Dark lesions along roots and stunted plant growth

causes_and_risk_factors: Warm, sandy soils with high soil moisture

favorable_conditions.soil_conditions: warm, sandy soils with high moisture

disease_development_and_spread: Nematodes feed on root tissues causing lesions

cultural_management: Crop rotation (using two consecutive resistant crops if levels are high)
Soil solarization during summer for 6-8 weeks
integrated_management: Combining field sanitation, crop rotation, genetic resistance, and soil solarization

warnings_and_limitations: Chemical nematicides may not be economically feasible, registered, or environmentally appropriate

general: Stems exhibit swelling and color changes from reddish-brown to black
Leaves and internodes show signs of necrosis
Young pods turn reddish-brown; seeds become darker, smaller, and distorted
visual_field_symptoms: Swollen, blackened stems and necrotic leaf/internode symptoms

field_identification: Reddish-brown to black swollen stems and necrotic lesions

causes_and_risk_factors: Temperate climate conditions, higher rainfall years
severity_and_yield_loss: Can potentially impact yield in years with higher rainfall

cultural_management: Using certified nematode-free seeds and planting materials

resistant_or_tolerant_varieties: Two tested lentil cultivars in South Australia demonstrated resistance
warnings_and_limitations: No lentil cultivars with resistance available in Europe

paper_level_notes: The paper covers a wide range of fungal, bacterial, viral, and nematode diseases affecting lentils globally, detailing their geographic distribution, symptoms, biology, epidemiology, and management strategies.
